hops.title: Cajal brings his own microscope to Berlin
hops.text: In October 1889, Santiago Ramón y Cajal, an anatomist little known outside Spain, went to the German Anatomical Society's congress in Berlin. His findings on separate nerve cells had met deep skepticism, so he packed his own Zeiss microscope, "brought just in case," in his words, with slides of cerebellum, retina and spinal cord. Arthur van Gehuchten, who was there, remembered Cajal standing alone, provoking only smiles of incredulity, until he took Rudolf Albert von Kölliker, the leading German histologist, aside and dragged him into a corner to look. By Cajal's account, Kölliker told him, "I have discovered you." Within a few months Kölliker had confirmed the findings.

sources.citation: DeFelipe J. Cajal and the discovery of the Golgi method: a neuroanatomist's dream. Anatomical Science International 100(4):384-399 (2025).

image.caption: Cajal carried his own Zeiss microscope to Berlin in 1889 so that sceptics could look for themselves.

hops.afterHeading: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells
hops.title: The giraffe nerve that takes the long way round
hops.text: In a giraffe, the nerve fibres that supply most laryngeal muscles take a detour. Before the neck forms, they lie just below the arteries near the heart. As the heart and great vessels descend into the chest, the fibres are dragged along. On the left they run down the neck in the vagus nerve, loop under the aortic arch and climb back in the recurrent laryngeal nerve. With a neck up to 2.4 metres, the full route approaches 5 metres, yet each fibre still grows from one nerve cell. For one giant sauropod, whose neck is estimated at 14 metres or more, the route probably exceeded 28 metres.

sources.citation: Wedel MJ. A monument of inefficiency: the presumed course of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in sauropod dinosaurs. Acta Palaeontologica Polonica 57(2):251-256 (2012).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A tall giraffe stretching its long spotted neck above an acacia tree on a sunlit savanna, with a small bird on a branch.
image.caption: A giraffe's left recurrent laryngeal nerve detours through the chest, yet each fibre grows from a single nerve cell.

hops.afterHeading: A pore is not a fusion
hops.title: A crayfish electrical synapse that favours one direction
hops.text: A gap junction can look like Golgi's net sneaking back in: a pore from one cell straight into the next, so surely current flows freely both ways. The first clear evidence for an electrical synapse says otherwise. In 1957 and 1959, Furshpan and Potter studied the crayfish escape circuit, whose giant neurons drive the emergency tail-flip. In Wine and Krasne's trials, the median time from stimulus marker to first spike was 4 milliseconds for medial giants and 7 milliseconds for lateral giants. At the synapse from the giant interneuron onto the giant motor neuron, voltage-dependent gating makes transmission rectifying: current passes forward far more easily than it flows back.

sources.citation: Herberholz J. The giant escape neurons of crayfish: past discoveries and present opportunities. Frontiers in Physiology 13:1052354 (2022).
Vaughn MJ, Haas JS. On the diverse functions of electrical synapses. Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience 16:910015 (2022).
Wine JJ, Krasne FB. The organization of escape behaviour in the crayfish. Journal of Experimental Biology 56(1):1-18 (1972).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A freshwater crayfish underwater in a rocky creek flicking its tail in a swirl of sand and bubbles.
image.caption: Crayfish giant neurons trigger the escape tail-flip through an electrical synapse that passes current mostly one way.
